figures.title: The Water and Ethanol Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Two small molecules: one you can’t live without, one you don’t need.

segments.name: Two Small Molecules
segments.text: This lesson finishes Module 1 with two small molecules that sit beside the big three. Water gives no calories at all, yet it's the nutrient you need most. Ethanol, the alcohol in drinks, gives calories, but your body has no use for it.

segments.name: The Water Branch
segments.text: On the left is water. We'll start with the molecule itself, which is bent and polar, and see why that lets it dissolve salts and sugars. Then we'll look at how much of your body is water, and how your body keeps the amount steady.
segments.cue: Left branch: Water and its four boxes

segments.name: The Ethanol Branch
segments.text: On the right is ethanol. Yeast makes it from sugar by fermentation. Its smaller cousin, methanol, is a poison. Then we'll follow ethanol into the liver, where it's broken down, and look at its effects. Each box links to the figure that explains it.
segments.cue: Right branch: Ethanol and its four boxes

segments.name: Why Water Matters
segments.text: You can live for weeks without food, but only a few days without water. It's the main ingredient of your body and of most whole foods.

segments.name: Ethanol and Labels
segments.text: Ethanol gives seven calories per gram, nearly as much as fat. Water only shows up in ingredient lists. In the US, most beer, wine and spirits are labeled under separate rules, so you see alcohol by volume rather than a Nutrition Facts panel.

figures.title: The Water Molecule
figures.subtitle: Bent, polar and sticky: why water dissolves so much.

segments.name: Two Hydrogens, One Oxygen
segments.text: Here's water: one oxygen in the middle, bonded to two hydrogens. Oxygen makes two bonds and hydrogen makes one, the same rules as in every lesson so far. Every atom is shown.

segments.name: Bent and Polar
segments.text: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself, so it ends up slightly negative and each hydrogen slightly positive. And the two bonds meet at about a hundred and four and a half degrees, so the molecule is bent like a V, not straight. One end negative, the other positive: chemists call that polar.

segments.name: Hydrogen Bonds
segments.text: Because of that, water molecules cling to each other. The slightly positive hydrogen of one is drawn to the slightly negative oxygen of the next. That's a hydrogen bond, shown as the dashed lines. Each one is weak and lasts only a split second, but there are so many that water stays liquid at body temperature and takes a lot of heat to warm up.

segments.name: Salts and Sugars Dissolve
segments.text: Polar water pulls table salt apart into sodium and chloride ions and wraps each one in water molecules. That's how minerals travel around your body. Sugars and many vitamins are covered in OH groups, which form hydrogen bonds with water, so they dissolve easily too.

segments.name: Fats Don’t
segments.text: Fat chains are just carbon and hydrogen, with no charge for water to grab. So oil and water separate. That's why fats need bile to be digested and protein carriers to travel in your blood, as we saw in the Fats lesson.

figures.title: Water in Your Body
figures.subtitle: How much of you is water, where it is, and what it does.

segments.name: How Much of You
segments.text: Water makes up about sixty percent of an adult man's body weight and around fifty to fifty-five percent of a woman's, because women on average carry more body fat, which holds little water. A newborn is about three quarters water. Muscle is about three quarters water too.

segments.name: Where It Is
segments.text: About two thirds of your body water is inside your cells. Most of the rest bathes the cells, and a smaller share is plasma, the liquid part of blood, which is over ninety percent water. Water moves freely between these spaces, following salts like sodium and potassium; that's one reason those minerals matter so much.

segments.name: Carrier and Coolant
segments.text: Water is the medium everything travels in: blood carries nutrients, oxygen, hormones and waste, and urine carries waste out. It also keeps your temperature steady. When sweat evaporates, it takes heat with it.

segments.name: Part of the Chemistry
segments.text: Water also takes part in chemistry. Every time you digest a protein or a starch, a water molecule is added back into each bond that's cut. That's hydrolysis. And water cushions your brain and spinal cord, lubricates your joints, and keeps your eyes and mouth moist.

figures.title: Water Balance
figures.subtitle: What comes in, what goes out, and how much you need.

segments.name: In and Out
segments.text: Most of your water comes from drinks, and all drinks count, including milk, tea and coffee. About a fifth comes from food, and your cells make roughly a cup a day as they burn fuel. Water leaves as urine, sweat, the moisture in every breath, and a little in stool. Heat, exercise, fever, vomiting and diarrhea all raise the losses.

segments.name: Keeping It Level
segments.text: When water runs low, your blood becomes slightly more concentrated. Your brain senses that and makes you thirsty, and the pituitary gland releases vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone. It tells the kidneys to save water, so urine becomes smaller in volume and darker. When you drink, the signals switch off.

segments.name: Water in Food
segments.text: Fruit and vegetables are mostly water. Cucumber, lettuce and celery are about ninety-five percent. Watermelon, strawberries and tomatoes are close behind. Even cooked oats and rice are mostly water, while bread is about a third and nuts very little.

segments.name: How Much You Need
segments.text: The US Institute of Medicine set an adequate intake for total water, from drinks and food together, of about two point seven liters a day for women and three point seven for men. About eighty percent of that usually comes from drinks. You need more in heat, with exercise, and when pregnant or breastfeeding.

segments.name: Too Little, Too Much
segments.text: Too little causes dehydration: thirst, dark urine, headache, tiredness and dizziness. Babies and older adults are most at risk, partly because older people feel thirst less. Too much, very fast, can dilute the sodium in your blood, called hyponatremia. That's rare, and mostly seen in long endurance events.

figures.title: Ethanol
figures.subtitle: From ethane to ethanol, how yeast makes it, and its toxic cousin.

segments.name: From Ethane
segments.text: Start with ethane: two carbons, each holding three hydrogens. Swap one of those hydrogens for an OH group, and you have ethanol. Any carbon chain carrying an OH like this is called an alcohol; ethanol is the one in drinks.

segments.name: Why It Spreads So Fast
segments.text: The OH lets ethanol mix with water, and the small carbon end lets it slip through fatty cell membranes. So it spreads quickly into every tissue, including the brain. It gives seven calories per gram but has no nutritional role.

segments.name: Fermentation
segments.text: Ethanol is made by yeast. Without oxygen, yeast splits each glucose into two ethanols and two carbon dioxides. Count the atoms: six carbons, twelve hydrogens and six oxygens on each side. Nothing is lost.
segments.cue: Glucose, arrow, ethanol and carbon dioxide

segments.name: Bread and Drinks
segments.text: In bread, the carbon dioxide makes the dough rise and most of the ethanol bakes off. In wine and beer, the ethanol stays. Very ripe fruit, fruit juice and fermented foods like kefir and kombucha contain small traces.

segments.name: Methanol
segments.text: Methanol is the simplest alcohol: the same OH on just one carbon. It's far more dangerous. Your liver turns it into formaldehyde and formic acid, which damage the optic nerve, so even small amounts of pure methanol can cause blindness or death. It's a danger in illegally distilled spirits. The tiny amounts in fruit juice are harmless.

figures.title: How Your Body Handles Alcohol
figures.subtitle: Absorbed fast, cleared slowly, in two steps in the liver.

segments.name: From Glass to Liver
segments.text: Some ethanol is absorbed in the stomach, and most in the small intestine, quickly. Food in the stomach slows it down. It then spreads through all your body water, which is why the same drink gives a smaller person a higher blood level. The liver clears roughly one standard drink an hour, and nothing speeds that up.

segments.name: Step One
segments.text: In the liver, an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase takes two hydrogens off ethanol. Look at the second carbon: it loses a hydrogen and the oxygen loses its hydrogen, leaving a C double bond O. That's acetaldehyde, a toxic, reactive molecule that causes much of alcohol's damage.

segments.name: Step Two
segments.text: A second enzyme, aldehyde dehydrogenase, adds an oxygen, making acetate, the same molecule that gives vinegar its sour taste. Cells burn acetate for energy or turn it into fat. Many people of East Asian descent carry a slow version of this second enzyme, so acetaldehyde builds up and their face flushes after even a small drink.
segments.cue: Acetic acid, marker 3, then the note

segments.name: One Standard Drink
segments.text: In the US, one standard drink has fourteen grams of pure ethanol. That's about twelve fluid ounces of beer at five percent, five ounces of wine at twelve percent, or one and a half ounces of spirits at forty percent.

segments.name: Effects
segments.text: In the short term, alcohol slows reactions and judgment, makes you urinate more by blocking vasopressin, and disturbs sleep. A lot at once can cause alcohol poisoning, which can be fatal. Heavy use over years damages the liver and heart, can lead to dependence, and often leaves people short of thiamine and folate. The World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies alcoholic drinks as a cause of cancer, and no amount is known to be safe in pregnancy. For health, less is better. This is general education, not medical advice.

figures.title: Where water and ethanol are used in the body
figures.subtitle: Tap a number on the cell to see what that part does; the list below it gives every other place in the body.

segments.name: Where Water and Ethanol Go
segments.text: Here's where water and ethanol are used or end up: first inside a single cell, then everywhere else in the body. Water is in every part of you, about 60% of an adult's weight. Ethanol is absorbed, burned for energy by the liver, and acts on the brain on the way.
segments.cue: The cell drawing and the list of places

segments.name: Inside a Cell
segments.text: Most of a cell is water, and that water is where its chemistry happens. Channels called aquaporins let water in and out, following the salts the cell pumps. Ethanol is different: liver cells break it down in steps. Enzymes in the cytosol and smooth ER turn it into acetaldehyde, which is toxic, and the mitochondria turn that into acetate. Heavy drinking crowds liver cells with fat droplets.
segments.cue: The cell drawing and its numbered parts

foodBody.name: Water
foodBody.text: From drinks and food; cells also make a little from burning fuel.

foodBody.name: Acetaldehyde
foodBody.text: The toxic step of alcohol breakdown; a common ALDH2 gene variant, frequent in East Asian people, slows its removal and causes flushing.

foodBody.name: Acetate
foodBody.text: The end product; it leaves the liver and is burned for energy by other tissues.

segments.name: Water Everywhere
segments.text: Blood plasma is about 90% water and carries nutrients, heat and wastes. About two thirds of your water is inside your cells, and muscle is about three quarters water. Joints are lubricated by a watery fluid.
segments.cue: In the list: blood, cells and joints

foodBody.name: Water
foodBody.text: Drinks, and food: fruit and vegetables are mostly water. Your body also makes a little when it burns food. It is the medium every chemical reaction in your cells happens in.

segments.name: Keeping the Balance
segments.text: The kidneys filter about 180 liters of fluid a day and return nearly all of it, keeping one or two liters as urine. Water also leaves as sweat and in your breath, and the large intestine takes back most of what's left in the gut.
segments.cue: In the list: kidneys, skin, large intestine and lungs

foodBody.name: Sodium
foodBody.text: Mostly from salt in food. In your body it holds water in the blood and the fluid around cells, so the kidneys balance water and sodium together.

foodBody.name: Alcohol
foodBody.text: It blocks vasopressin, the hormone that tells the kidneys to hold on to water, so you pass more urine while alcohol is in your blood.

segments.name: The Path of Alcohol
segments.text: A little alcohol is absorbed in the stomach, and most in the small intestine. The liver breaks most of it down, to acetaldehyde and then acetate, at about one drink an hour. On the way, alcohol reaches the brain and slows nerve signals, and a little leaves in your breath.
segments.cue: In the list: stomach, small intestine, liver, brain and lungs

foodBody.name: Ethanol
foodBody.text: The alcohol in beer, wine and spirits. Your liver burns it for energy, about 7 kcal per gram, but it is not a nutrient, and less is better for health.

foodBody.name: Acetaldehyde
foodBody.text: Not something you eat: your liver makes it from ethanol. It is toxic and causes much of a hangover, and the liver quickly turns it into acetate.

segments.name: Simplified
segments.text: This is simplified. Every cell holds water, and alcohol spreads through all body water, so the list gives each place's main job, not every detail. Body water and the rate alcohol is cleared vary from person to person.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here's every molecule in this lesson in one table: its formula, its energy, what it does in your body and where you find it. Notice that ethanol's breakdown products, acetaldehyde and acetate, are molecules you've already met on this page.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. Coffee and tea still count toward your water. Ice floats because hydrogen bonds hold it in an open lattice. Cooking doesn't remove all the alcohol from a dish; a long simmer removes most, but rarely all. And in the US, a non-alcoholic drink can still contain up to half a percent alcohol. That's Module 1.
